\section[el gobierno]{el gobierno — the government}

\label{lesson:ES-C601-gobierno}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the citizen, then the Spanish for to belong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el gobierno}
\textbf{el gobierno} — \textquotedblleft{}the government\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El gobierno subió los impuestos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The government raised taxes.}
\end{quote}

The verb is \emph{gobernar} (e$\to$ie).

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gobierno} is built on \emph{gobernar}, inherited from Latin \emph{gubernare} 'to steer' (EtymDB), a verb Latin took from Greek \emph{kybernan} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el gobierno}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el gobierno}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el gobierno}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the citizen, then the Spanish for to belong, then say \emph{el gobierno} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el gobierno mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The government\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la política]{la política — the politics; the policy}

\label{lesson:ES-C601-politica}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to belong, then the Spanish for the government.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la política}
\textbf{la política} — \textquotedblleft{}the politics; the policy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No me interesa la política.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am not interested in politics.}
\end{quote}

Also a policy: \emph{la política de la empresa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{la política} is a learned borrowing from Greek \emph{politikē} 'the affairs of the city', built on \emph{polis} 'city', through Latin \emph{politicus} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la política}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la política}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la política}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to belong, then the Spanish for the government, then say \emph{la política} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la política mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The politics; the policy\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[político]{político — political; the politician}

\label{lesson:ES-C601-politico}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the government, then the Spanish for the politics.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: político}
\textbf{político} — \textquotedblleft{}political; the politician\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Es un tema político.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is a political issue.}
\end{quote}

As a noun: \emph{el político, la política} — the politician.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{político} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{politicus}, taken from Greek \emph{politikos} 'of citizens, of the state', built on \emph{polis} 'city' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the government, then the Spanish for the politics, then say \emph{político} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[el ministro]{el ministro — the minister}

\label{lesson:ES-C601-ministro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the politics, then the Spanish for political.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el ministro}
\textbf{el ministro} — \textquotedblleft{}the minister\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El ministro habló en la tele.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The minister spoke on TV.}
\end{quote}

A woman is \emph{la ministra}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ministro} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{minister} 'servant, helper' (EtymDB), built on \emph{minus} 'less' as \emph{magister} is on \emph{magis}: the lesser one who serves (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el ministro}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el ministro}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the politics, then the Spanish for political, then say \emph{el ministro} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[el concejal]{el concejal — the town councillor}

\label{lesson:ES-C601-concejal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for political, then the Spanish for the minister.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el concejal}
\textbf{el concejal} — \textquotedblleft{}the town councillor\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La concejala abrió la nueva biblioteca.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The councillor opened the new library.}
\end{quote}

A woman is \emph{la concejala}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{concejal} is built on \emph{concejo} 'town council', inherited from Latin \emph{concilium} 'assembly, meeting' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
